sentence: Faculty participants rated the male applicant as significantly more competent and hireable than the identical female applicant.
Faculty also offered a higher starting salary and more career mentoring to the male applicant.
The gender of the faculty participants did not affect responses, such that female and male faculty were equally likely to exhibit bias against the female student.
Mediation analyses indicated that the female student was less likely to be hired because she was viewed as less competent.
Despite efforts to recruit and retain more women, a stark gender disparity persists within academic science.
The bias appears to be unintentional, generated from widespread cultural stereotypes rather than a conscious intention to harm women.
Women remain underrepresented in academic science, particularly at senior levels, even in fields where they earn over half of doctorates.
Cultural stereotypes portray women as less competent in science, technology, engineering, and mathematics compared to men.
Stereotypes that depict women as less capable in science contribute to faculty perceptions that female students are less qualified than male students.
Implicit assumptions that men are more naturally suited to scientific work shape evaluations even when applicant qualifications are identical.
Faculty endorsement of subtle bias against women predicted lower competence ratings, lower hireability ratings, and reduced mentoring of the female student.
The pervasive view that women lack the ability needed to succeed in science continues to disadvantage female trainees.
Women constitute approximately half of doctoral graduates in the life sciences yet hold a much smaller share of tenure-track positions.
At the postdoctoral and faculty levels, women remain underrepresented across the biological, physical, and engineering sciences.
The leaky pipeline metaphor describes the disproportionate loss of women at successive stages of the academic career.
Female scientists are awarded fewer grants, receive lower salaries, and are promoted more slowly than their male counterparts with comparable records.
Even at top research universities, the proportion of women on the faculty in physics and engineering remains below twenty percent.
We recruited faculty participants from Biology, Chemistry, and Physics departments at three public and three private research-intensive universities in the United States.
Participants completed the materials online and were compensated with a thirty-dollar Amazon gift card.
Application materials were created based on prior empirical work and pilot tested for realism.
Participants rated the applicant on a seven-point scale measuring competence, hireability, and likability.
All analyses were conducted using SPSS version 19, with alpha set at 0.05.
The institutional review board at Yale University approved all procedures prior to data collection.
The final sample consisted of 127 faculty members from a range of academic ranks and subfields.
